# Bridge: industry exposure, "could" versus "does" (RQ2) {#sec-rq2}

RQ2 asks a descriptive question: across the {{< var design.n_industries >}} FF49 industries, how far does the ranking by observed usage of the model stand from the ranking by theoretical exposure? Nothing in this section is a hypothesis test or a decision (PAP §2.0). The AEI side of each comparison is built from conversations matched to O\*NET tasks, carried to occupations and then to industries; the "could" side is a published exposure score carried to the same industries. The index definitions are in @sec-data and the bootstrap in @sec-methods; this section reports what they produce for Design B.

## Three industry indices

The industry indices share one construction (@sec-data). An occupation's usage intensity is its share of AEI usage divided by its share of US employment; its delegation intensity is that usage intensity multiplied by the occupation's automation share, and its augmentation intensity is the same product with the augmentation share. Each industry index is the employment-weighted sum of an intensity over the occupations the industry employs, with OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights, standardised across the {{< var design.n_industries >}} industries to give `z_usage`, `z_delegation` and `z_augmentation`. Delegation and augmentation exposure are therefore usage exposure split by collaboration mode, and they sit close to each other in rank. Softw, Books, Aero, Guns and Hardw head all three rankings, and Meals, Rtail, Cnstr and Coal sit at the foot of all three (@tbl-rq2-top-bottom-usage, @tbl-rq2-top-bottom-delegation, @tbl-rq2-top-bottom-augmentation; @sec-app-supplementary). Where the orderings differ, they differ in the middle of the cross-section and in the order within these groups, not in which industries are at either end.

The distribution of the industry scores is strongly skewed. {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max_industry >}} holds the largest delegation z-score, {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max >}} SD, against {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_2nd >}} SD for the next industry and {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_min >}} SD at the bottom; the skewness of the {{< var design.n_industries >}} delegation scores is {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_skewness >}}, and that of the usage scores {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_usage_skewness >}} (@tbl-audit-exposure-coverage; @sec-app-supplementary). Softw's benchmark exposures are also high (@tbl-rq2-top-bottom-delegation), but on the AEI side it stands much further from the rest of the cross-section. A rank correlation suits such a distribution, since it reads Softw as first and no more; the same skew is why the market tests carry a ranks row and a drop-Softw row beside the primary (@sec-markets).

## Could versus does

@tbl-rq2-could-vs-does-b reports the Spearman correlation of each AEI index with each benchmark, with industry-bootstrap percentile intervals over {{< var rq2.n_draws >}} draws. The headline benchmark is the Eloundou et al. human-annotator β [@eloundou2024gpts], with the GPT-4 β (`z_eloundou_gpt4`) beside it in every row (PAP D8). The human rating does not rest on a language model's judgement of language-model exposure; the GPT-4 one does. Making the GPT-4 β the headline is R17, which reorders the same table and changes no value (@sec-app-robustness-tables). The headline correlation of delegation exposure with the human β is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}]; with the GPT-4 β beside it, it is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.hi >}}]. Against the Felten, Raj and Seamans AIOE [@felten2021occupational] it is {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_aioe.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_aioe.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_delegation.z_aioe.ci.hi >}}]. AIOE is scored on an earlier SOC vintage and reaches the current SOC codes of OEWS through the O\*NET-detail union crosswalk as built (PAP D6); R14 replaces it with the published BLS SOC vintage crosswalk [@bls2018soccrosswalk]. Every value here is Design B with OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights, which are not strictly real-time (S1, set out below).

{{< include _generated/tables/rq2-could-vs-does-b.md >}}

For usage exposure the correlations are {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}] with the human β, {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou_gpt4.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.hi >}}] with the GPT-4 β and {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_aioe.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_aioe.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_usage.z_aioe.ci.hi >}}] with AIOE; for augmentation exposure they are {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}], {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou_gpt4.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.hi >}}] and {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_aioe.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_aioe.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.b.z_augmentation.z_aioe.ci.hi >}}] (@tbl-rq2-could-vs-does-b; Design B, OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights, not strictly real-time, S1). Within each benchmark, delegation exposure has the lowest point correlation and augmentation exposure the highest; within each AEI index, the human β gives the lowest and the GPT-4 β the highest, with AIOE between them. These orderings describe point estimates only. The intervals are wide for a sample of {{< var design.n_industries >}} industries and they overlap throughout the table; they describe spread and do not test one correlation against another.

@fig-rq2-could-vs-does plots delegation exposure against each benchmark, one point per industry. Most industries lie along a common increasing band. Softw sits apart at the top right of every panel. Fin, Banks and Insur sit apart in the other direction, far along each benchmark axis but near the middle of the delegation axis, and Rtail, RlEst and Hlth lie below the band.

## What the correlation shares, and what it assumes

Two features of the construction bear on how far apart "could" and "does" appear. First, both sides of every ρ inherit the same OEWS occupation-to-industry weights: the AEI indices and the AIOE and Eloundou benchmarks are each aggregated to industries with the same matrix (PAP §11). Two industries that employ similar occupations therefore receive similar scores on both sides, whatever the occupation-level agreement between usage and theoretical exposure, so part of each correlation in @tbl-rq2-could-vs-does-b is common occupational mix rather than agreement between the two kinds of measure. Second, ρ depends on the D3 zero assumption. Occupations with no AEI match are unpublished in AEI and are assigned zero usage by assumption (D3); they are not measured as zero. They hold {{< var d3.zero_assigned_pct >}}% of OEWS employment under Design B (@sec-data). R3 drops them instead, and R3 lowers ρ most among the RQ2 robustness rows: the headline correlation of delegation exposure with the human β falls to {{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}] (@sec-app-robustness-tables; Design B, OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights, not strictly real-time, S1).

The timing caveat S1 applies to every Spearman in this section (PAP §10 S1). Design B's OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights were released on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after the {{< var design.formation >}} formation date and inside the return window, and the O\*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}} task links also postdate formation, although their task text is byte-identical to that of {{< var vintage.onet.r32 >}} (PAP §11, C-74). Design B is out of sample in its AEI data only; it is not strictly real-time (PAP §2.1). The strict real-time row R32 uses OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r32 >}} weights; it is a market row and reports no RQ2 Spearman, so no RQ2 value under strict real-time inputs exists (@sec-markets, @sec-app-robustness-tables). R1, with OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r1 >}} weights, is labelled look-ahead; its headline correlation is {{< var rob.r01.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r01.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r01.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}].

## Where "could" and "does" part

@tbl-rq2-rank-gaps-eloundou (@sec-app-supplementary) lists the industries whose rank on delegation exposure differs most from their rank on the human β, with the GPT-4 β and AIOE versions in @tbl-rq2-rank-gaps-eloundou-gpt4 and @tbl-rq2-rank-gaps-aioe (Design B, OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights, not strictly real-time, S1). The industries that rank higher on "could" than on "does" are trade, real estate, health, transport and finance: Rtail, RlEst, Whlsl, Hlth and Trans head the list against the human β, Rtail and RlEst head it against all three benchmarks, and Fin, Banks and Insur sit near the top of each theoretical ranking but in the upper middle of the delegation ranking. The industries that rank higher on "does" than on "could" are mostly manufacturing: against the human β the list ends with Txtls and Autos, preceded by FabPr, Steel, Mach and BldMt, and Txtls ends it against all three benchmarks. Read together with the correlations, the picture is broad agreement in the ordering of industries, with sizeable disagreement for a set of service and finance industries on one side and several manufacturing industries on the other.

The delegation index also carries measurement uncertainty from AEI's suppression of small cells. @tbl-rq2-bounds-industries and @fig-rq2-bound-widths (@sec-app-supplementary) report each industry's delegation exposure between its lower and upper suppression bounds. Relative to the index level, the bounds are widest for Other, Rtail, Coal and Cnstr, which lie at the bottom of the delegation ranking, and narrowest for Softw, Txtls, Hardw and Books. Rtail thus shows both a large positive rank gap and one of the widest relative bounds; the tables record both and attach no interpretation to their coincidence.

{{< include _generated/figures/rq2-bound-widths.md >}}

Exploratory and look-ahead: Design `A_pooled`, which pools later releases (PAP §10 S3), gives a correlation of delegation exposure with the human β of {{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou.ci.hi >}}] and with the GPT-4 β of {{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.rho >}} [{{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.lo >}}, {{< var rq2.a_pooled.z_delegation.z_eloundou_gpt4.ci.hi >}}] (@tbl-rq2-could-vs-does-a-pooled; @sec-app-supplementary). Its zero-assigned share under D3 is {{< var audit.zero_assigned_pct.a_pooled >}}% of employment, again unpublished in AEI and assigned zero by assumption, not measured as zero.

## Robustness rows for RQ2

The pre-registered RQ2 robustness rows are reported in full in @sec-app-robustness-tables and summarised in @sec-robustness; each is robustness and none is a decision (PAP §8.1). For the headline pair, delegation exposure against the human β, the values are as follows. R1 (OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r1 >}} weights, look-ahead) gives {{< var rob.r01.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}}; R2 (wage-bill weights) {{< var rob.r02.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r02.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r02.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}]; R3 (occupations without AEI usage dropped, D3) {{< var rob.r03.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}}; R11 (employment-weighted task allocation, D4) {{< var rob.r11.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r11.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r11.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}]; R20 (the `majority` crosswalk mode in place of `split`) {{< var rob.r20.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r20.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r20.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}]; and R33 (the employment-weighted NAICS to SIC crosswalk, D23) {{< var rob.r33.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r33.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r33.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}]. Each except R1 is a Design B construction under the S1 timing caveat above; R1 is look-ahead.

Three rows leave the headline pair at its primary value, for reasons the PAP records. R14 changes only the AIOE crosswalk (D6), so it moves the AIOE column, to {{< var rob.r14.spearman_z_aioe_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} [{{< var rob.r14.spearman_z_aioe_vs_z_delegation.ci_lo >}}, {{< var rob.r14.spearman_z_aioe_vs_z_delegation.ci_hi >}}] for delegation exposure, and leaves the Eloundou columns at {{< var rob.r14.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}}. R15 redistributes NAICS head-office employment by the same fraction of every industry, which leaves every rank, and so every Spearman, at the primary value of {{< var rob.r15.spearman_z_eloundou_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} (PAP §11, C-70). R17 makes the GPT-4 β the headline and changes no value: delegation exposure against the GPT-4 β stays at {{< var rob.r17.spearman_z_eloundou_gpt4_vs_z_delegation.estimate >}} (PAP D8; @sec-app-robustness-tables).
